item.title: Apple seeks engineer to lead development of new agentic AI assistant
item.description:
Apple seeks engineer to lead development of new agentic AI assistant

Apple is working on an AI agent capable of performing a range of tasks, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. This development is being pursued by Apple, which is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant, according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg.

🔍 Overview

Apple’s initiative puts the company in a position to compete with other agentic AI offerings. The new agent is designed to operate fluidly between various digital tools, such as a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, and a service. The goal is to build agents that plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, while coordinating specialized sub-agents.

🧩 How it works

The job listing details that the engineer will work closely with teams across Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions. The system is intended to coordinate specialized sub-agents to complete complex tasks.

⚙️ Key details

  • The AI agent will be able to browse the web, work across apps, and call services.
  • The role involves planning and carrying out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.
  • The agent will coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.
  • Apple has already rolled out its AI-upgraded Siri, which allows users to ask questions about what is on their screen and perform actions across apps.
  • Reports suggest Apple could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs.

🚀 Availability

Apple is rolling out an upcoming iOS 27.3 update that gives developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into all apps. This feature is currently part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

#Apple #AIagents #Siri #Bloomberg

Source: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent

item.title: Google adds collapsible AI chat sidebar to homepage
item.description:
Google adds collapsible AI chat sidebar to homepage

Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches by adding a collapsible sidebar that allows users to view and continue their AI chats. This change introduces a new way to access recent AI Mode activities directly from the Google homepage, moving beyond the traditional single search bar.

🔍 Overview

The update integrates AI chat functionality directly into the Google homepage experience. Previously, users accessed AI features through the AI Mode button in the search bar, which opened a chatbot-like search experience. The new interface adds a persistent sidebar to manage these interactions.

🧩 How it works

Users can open the sidebar by clicking a gray bar that appears on the left side of the screen. From there, the interface displays a list of recent searches made using AI Mode. The sidebar provides tools to manage these conversations and initiate new interactions.

⚙️ Key details

The new sidebar includes the following features:

  • View a list of recent searches made using AI Mode
  • Start a new thread
  • Search existing threads
  • Connect a Gemini Notebook

This update follows other recent changes to Google’s search box, which in May was updated to accommodate longer queries and include AI-powered autocomplete. Last year, Google brought its AI Mode button to the search bar.

🚀 Availability

The new homepage layout is rolling out globally on desktop.

💡 Why it matters

Robby Stein, Google’s vice president of product, stated that the option is being rolled out because “people are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done.” Stein added that “in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.”

#Google #AI #Search #ProductUpdates

Source: Google is putting AI chats right on the homepage

item.title: Evaluating When Offline Tests Can Replace A/B Experiments
item.description:
Evaluating When Offline Tests Can Replace A/B Experiments

In our paper, When Can You Ship on Evals Alone?, we work through this problem in detail.

🔍 Overview

  • When we change an AI feature, say a new prompt or a different underlying LLM, there are two main ways to check whether it got better.
  • Offline evals are quick tests run on a fixed set of sample prompts before any real user sees the change, often with other LLM-as-judges grading the answers.
  • A/B tests give the new version to a random group of real users and compare how they behave against users on the old version.
  • The potential upside is substantial.
  • Offline evals take hours; A/B tests often take days or weeks.

📈 Why offline evals matter

  • If we could confidently make product decisions based on offline evals alone, we could shorten feedback loops and iterate much faster.

⚙️ Formal problem definition

  • We formalize the “when we can ship based on eval alone” as follows: We want to make shipping decisions based on the offline eval while bounding the risk of shipping something that actually harms the online metric.
  • If we want to bound the risk of shipping something that harms the online metric, ideally we need to know the conditional distribution of the true online treatment effect, given the observed offline eval treatment effect.
  • We cannot have a heterogeneous set of experiments where, for some types of changes, an improvement in the eval corresponds to an improvement in the online outcome, while for others the relationship is different or even reversed.

📊 Noise and correlation

  • Both numbers are noisy estimates, not exact values.
  • Offline eval scores have sampling errors from several sources, including randomly sampling examples from a larger eval set, and using an LLM to grade the answers (LLM-as-a-judge).
  • Online treatment effects are estimated with sampling error too.
  • The short version: if we ignore noise, a strong offline-online relation can look weak.
  • The squared correlation (R², roughly how much of the online result the eval explains, from 0 to 100%) determines how much uncertainty remains in the online effect after observing the eval.
  • A high R² means the eval is highly informative about the online outcome.
  • A low R² means substantial uncertainty remains, regardless of how precisely we measure the eval.
  • Using a naive estimator, we find that the squared correlation is only 24% in the working example.
  • In our example, a naive estimate says the eval explains 24% of the variation in online results, when the true figure is 60%.
  • Noise is a problem too, because it can hide a strong link between offline and online results.

🛠️ Assumptions

  • We assume that we have a sufficiently large, homogeneous pool of paired offline eval effects and online treatment effects.
  • And, we assume that any future changes for which we want to make eval-based decisions come from the same class, with the same underlying relationship between offline and online effects (also called exchangeability).
  • We assume that the true offline and online treatment effects follow a bivariate normal distribution.
  • We assume that measurement errors are centered at zero with known variances, independent across interventions.
  • We assume that any errors introduced by using an LLM as a judge are independent of the treatment arm.

#offline-evals #ab-testing #ai-evaluation

Source: When Can You Ship on Offline Evals Alone? | Spotify Engineering

item.title: Audible introduces AI-assisted audio discovery for audiobooks
item.description:
Audible introduces AI-assisted audio discovery for audiobooks

Audible is introducing a new AI-assisted audio discovery feature designed to help users determine whether they will enjoy an audiobook before starting to listen. The update aims to prevent users from needing to research titles on other platforms by providing a soundbite synopsis.

🔍 Overview

The new feature combines audiobook samples, AI overviews, and author commentary to give users more information before choosing their next story. It also includes recommended audiobook collections personalized to individual listening tastes.

“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend. With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you, from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author,” Audible chief product officer Andy Tsao said in the announcement. “Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily.”

🧩 How it works

Audio discovery plays users a snippet of the audiobook along with a brief AI-generated overview. This overview includes the book’s themes and listener reactions, drawing from reviews and other publicly available data. The feature can also include commentary from an author or Audible editor, which is pulled directly from past Audible interviews.

In addition to audio discovery, Audible is using AI to personalize audiobook collections around users’ listening tastes. These collections are intended to make titles that do not appear on best-selling lists easier to discover.

⚙️ Key details

Audible is also expanding two existing beta features as part of this update:

  • Ask a Question: Allows users to ask AI about characters, plot points, references, and more.
  • Recaps: Provides spoiler-free audio summaries of what the user has already listened to.

These expanded features are available for a “select set” of additional English-language titles in the US, with a broader rollout planned to start in December.

🚀 Availability

Audio discovery and the personalized collections are rolling out on select English-language titles in the US, with plans to eventually expand to other regions. Like audio discovery, the personalized collections are rolling out to customers in the US and also include commentary from Audible’s editors.

💡 Why it matters

These are the latest AI-powered features that Audible is introducing in an effort to attract new users and fend off growing competition from rival platforms like Spotify.

#Audible #AIAssisted #AudioDiscovery #Personalization #Streaming

Source: Audible is trying to make it easier to find audiobooks you’ll actually like
